source.title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
source.authors: Shreya Saha; Benjamin K. Bergen; Meenakshi Khosla

page_placements.theme: Neuron basis is privileged by the activation function and training; rotation removes unit-level interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The study directly examines unit-level versus subspace-level functional separation and argues that the absence of specialized individual units does not establish that a network lacks modular organization. It refines the claim by distinguishing unit-level modularity from subspace-level modularity.
record.gate_note: The vision and language retrieval tests compare unit-aligned (permutation), orthogonal, and invertible decompositions. They do not measure individual neurons' responses to the example inputs in the claim or estimate a general prevalence of polysemantic neurons. The study's text also reports qualitative cross-architecture vision findings; detailed model-by-model values in the flattened appendix table are not transcribed here. The RNN findings concern unit specialization and task-selective ablation, rather than vision or language neuron response rates.
record.test_reason: The study tests functional modularity: whether two broad computations (content vs style, syntax vs semantics, task A vs task B) can be separated by a permutation, rotation or invertible linear map, judged by retrieval or ablation. It does not measure whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs or features. The authors also say their notion is 'distinct from distributed coding and superposition'. The permutation-level failures show that two dimensions of the same input are mixed across units. That is a mixed-selectivity or modularity construct, not a rate of polysemantic neurons. The RNN FTV result concerns task-variance specialization of units in cognitive-task CTRNNs, with Yang et al. replicated. It is not a share of polysemantic neurons in classifiers or transformers. These findings are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as tests of V1, V2 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that absence of unit-level modularity often coexists with subspace-level (orthogonal or linear) functional modularity across RNNs, vision and language models, enabling targeted intervention. They explicitly separate this from superposition and distributed coding, and note that the vision and language results rest on retrieval rather than behavioural ablation.
record.recipe_differences: Learns permutation, orthogonal, or invertible linear decompositions with task-sufficiency or contrastive objectives; evaluates vision and language representations mainly by retrieval, rather than the original neuron-level feature investigation. RNN decompositions additionally use causal subspace ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: Transformation family changes measured separation (permutation, orthogonal, invertible); activation function changes unit-level FTV and DDI in Yang RNNs; the ResNet family is an exception for style retrieval.

fits_no_version.finding: Unit-aligned (permutation) decompositions give near-chance separation of content vs style in vision models (Swin Base Rs≈1.10, Rc≈1.02) and the weakest separation of syntax vs semantics in LMs. Invertible linear subspaces separate them strongly (Rs=16.1, Rc=5.3). The pattern holds across Swin, ConvNeXt, VGG and ViT/DINO; ResNets are the exception for style.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixed unit-level selectivity (units carrying several functions) coexists with functionally separable linear subspaces, so lack of monosemantic units does not imply lack of modularity.

fits_no_version.finding: In Yang multitask RNNs, unit task specialization depends on activation: softplus has 74% specialized units, tanh 30%. Unit-level ablation gives DDI 0.59 (softplus) vs 0.00 (tanh), yet tanh networks reach DDI 0.37 (orthogonal) and 0.47 (linear). Mante tanh RNNs show DDI≈0.28 only under linear decomposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation function changes how far task computations align with unit axes; non-aligned networks still hold causally separable task subspaces.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
record.problems: Vision and language modularity is assessed with retrieval selectivity rather than causal behavioral intervention; these experiments use single splits and the text says error bars cannot be provided for sections 1 and 2. The paper reports sensitivity to decomposition hyperparameters and notes ResNet-family weakness for style retrieval. The study does not directly measure neuron responses to the example inputs or estimate population-wide polysemantic-neuron prevalence.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the detailed numeric entries in Appendix Table E11 and the additional language-model table/figure results in Appendix E12 and Figures E16–E18; they are cross-model or layer-specific retrieval results, while the retained rows capture the main unit-aligned versus subspace comparison and the stated architecture exception. Also omitted RNN Mante-task rows because the listed claim versions do not cover those task results.

untested.parts: No individual-neuron response analysis in image classifiers; content/style mixing across units is a different construct.
No MLP-neuron token/context response rates and no layerwise share of polysemantic neurons. The layer results in Fig E18 concern subspace retrieval.
Superposition is discussed only to distinguish it from modularity; not tested.
No SoLU or convnet polysemantic-neuron share and no performance trade-off. The only activation comparison is task specialization of RNN units.
Not tested. The study shows that modularity depends on level of description, not that neuron polysemanticity labels depend on activation range or scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links to V1, V2 and V5 and all its labels are dropped because the study's measures concern functional modularity, not polysemantic neurons. Neither original source is involved. Results not captured by rows (Table E11 cross-model vision metrics, Table E12 Pythia 160M and GPT-2 XL, the Mante RNN results, and the E.9 controls) also bear only on the fits_no_version findings. Table E4 shows the inclusive and mixed Yang task pairs stay non-modular (max DDI ≤0.05).

versions.untested_parts: Tests content–style unit-aligned retrieval separation in vision representations, not specific neurons or the example cat-face/car/cat-leg stimuli, nor prevalence across image classifiers generally.
Tests syntax–semantics retrieval in selected language-model representations, not MLP-specific activations, token-level response prevalence, or a large-share estimate across language models.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons or by superposition.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

Tests activation-function differences in Yang multitask RNN unit specialization and dissociation; does not compare SoLU, modern convnets' polysemantic-neuron share, or performance costs of reducing that share.
Does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons for a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
Does not vary activation-range sampling or explanation-scoring methods to assess whether polysemanticity classification depends on measurement choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It mentions mixed selectivity and superposition (lines 115-116, 139-155) but does not test or use any polysemanticity version.

tranche.reason: Study measures functional modularity (FTV task specialization, DDI under unit/subspace ablation, retrieval selectivity). It reports no rate of neurons responding to unrelated features; it explicitly separates its question from superposition.

source_check.notes: All nine rows match the text; values come from the authors' own 256-unit CTRNNs on Yang's 11 tasks, Anti vs DM1 pair only. The text calls 0.59->0.73->0.70 'increasing' though linear (0.70) is below orthogonal (0.73). The softplus-vs-tanh FTV contrast is a near-miss for V5 (task-level mixed selectivity, not feature polysemanticity), so T6 holds.

statements.problem: none; 74%/30% specialized (|FTV|>0.5) and DDI 0.59/0.00/0.37/0.47 match Section 3.1 for the Anti vs DM1 pair

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Permutation decomposition has near-chance selectivity, which the authors interpret as content and style not being separable at the unit level (r1–r8). This is evidence about these tested properties, not the example neuron or a general rate of polysemantic neurons.
